'''Michael T. Avery''' (February 15, 1952{{spaced ndash}}August 30, 2023) was a [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] politician who served as a member of the [[Nebraska Legislature]] from the 3rd district from 1993 to 1997. He was originally elected as a [[Nebraska Democratic Party|Democrat]], but later switched to the [[Nebraska Republican Party|Republican Party]].<ref name="nine republicans">{{cite news|last=Reed|first=Leslie|title=Nine Republicans seek Bruning's Legislature seat|newspaper=[[Omaha World-Herald]]|date=November 13, 2002|location=|page=16|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/omaha-world-herald/191636648/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=April 11, 2026}}</ref>

==Early life==
Avery was born in [[Newcastle, Wyoming]], and graduated from Crawford High School in [[Crawford, Nebraska]], in 1970.<ref name="Nebraska legislature">{{cite news|title=Nebraska Legislature|newspaper=[[Omaha World-Herald]]|date=October 29, 1992|location=|page=41|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/omaha-world-herald/191635550/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref><ref name="blue book">{{cite book|title=Nebraska Blue Book 1992-93|editor-last1=Meyer|editor-first1=Judy A.|publisher=Clerk of the Nebraska Legislature|date=1993|url=https://govdocs.nebraska.gov/epubs/l3000/D001-199293.pdf|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> He attended the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln|University of Nebraska]], graduating with his bachelor's degree.<ref name="Nebraska legislature"/><ref name="blue book"/> He worked as a fish and wildlife biologist and aquatic education coordinator for the [[Nebraska Game and Parks Commission]].<ref name="blue book"/>

In 1980, Avery ran for the [[Gretna, Nebraska|Gretna]] City Council from Ward I.<ref>{{cite news|title=Avery Petitions For Council Seat|newspaper=Gretna Guide and News|date=August 13, 1980|location=|page=1|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/gretna-guide-and-news/191635707/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> He defeated Ruth Houser in the election, receiving 57 percent of the vote to her 43 percent.<ref>{{cite news|title=City Council Has Two New Members|newspaper=Gretna Guide and News|date=November 12, 1980|location=|page=1|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/gretna-guide-and-news/191635936/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> He was re-elected unopposed in 1984.<ref>{{cite news|title=Sarpy County|newspaper=[[Omaha World-Herald]]|date=November 7, 1984|location=|page=15|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/omaha-world-herald/191636034/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> In 1988, Avery ran for Mayor and was elected unopposed.<ref>{{cite news|last=Dahlheim|first=Gregg|title=Voter registration sets record in Sarpy|newspaper=Gretna Guide and News|date=November 2, 1988|location=|page=1|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/gretna-guide-and-news/191636065/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref>

==Nebraska Legislature==
In 1992, State Senator [[Emil Beyer (Nebraska politician)|Emil Beyer]] declined to seek re-election,<ref>{{cite news|last=Gertzen|first=Jason|title=Chizek Not Seeking Re-election; Says Political Career Isn't Over|newspaper=[[Omaha World-Herald]]|date=February 28, 1992|location=|page=24|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/omaha-world-herald/191633663/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> and Avery ran to succeed him in the 3rd district,<ref>{{cite news|last1=Ivey|first1=James|last2=Hendee|first2=David|title=10 Candidates File For 3rd District Seat|newspaper=[[Omaha World-Herald]]|date=March 14, 1992|location=|page=8|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/omaha-world-herald/191633707/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> which included most of [[Sarpy County, Nebraska|Sarpy County]] in [[Omaha–Council Bluffs metropolitan area|metropolitan Omaha]]. In a crowded primary,<ref>{{cite news|last=Ivey|first=James|title=3rd District Race Up for Grabs|newspaper=[[Omaha World-Herald]]|date=April 13, 1992|location=|page=9|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/omaha-world-herald/191634469/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> former Sarpy County Planning Commissioner Lynda Thorpe placed first with 26 percent of the vote. Avery narrowly beat out businessman Bob Twiss for second place, receiving 3 votes more than Twiss,<ref name="1992 results">{{cite book|title=Official Report of the Nebraska State Canvassing Board, Primary Election, May 12, 1992, General Election, November 3, 1992|last=Beermann|first=Allen J.|publisher=Nebraska Secretary of State|year=1992|url=https://govdocs.nebraska.gov/epubs/S1200/S001-1992prim_gen.pdf|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> which was confirmed by a recount.<ref>{{cite news|last=Ivey|first=James|title=Four Close Nebraska Races Are Unchanged by Recounts|newspaper=[[Omaha World-Herald]]|date=June 11, 1992|location=|page=13|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/omaha-world-herald/191634780/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> In the general election, Avery defeated Thorpe, winning 53 percent of the vote to Thorpe's 37 percent.<ref name="1992 results"/>

Avery ran for re-election in 1996 and was challenged by Richard Bellino, a businessman, and [[Jon Bruning]], a business development consultant and attorney.<ref>{{cite news|last=Blackwood|first=Kendrick|title=District 3 Rivals Say Smaller Is Best|newspaper=[[Omaha World-Herald]]|date=May 8, 1996|location=|page=44|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/omaha-world-herald/191635035/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> Avery placed first in the primary, winning 47 percent of the vote to Bruning's 39 percent and Bellino's 14 percent.<ref name="1996 results">{{cite book|title=Official Report of the Board of State Canvassers of the State of Nebraska, Primary Election, May 14, 1996, General Election, November 5, 1996|last=Moore|first=Scott|publisher=Nebraska Secretary of State|year=1996|url=https://govdocs.nebraska.gov/epubs/S1200/S001-1996prim_gen.pdf|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> In the general election, the ''[[Omaha World-Herald]]'' endorsed Bruning over Avery, criticizing Avery's "relatively low profile" and his abstentions on pieces of legislation.<ref>{{cite news|title=Change Recommended in Legislature|newspaper=[[Omaha World-Herald]]|date=October 23, 1996|location=|page=24|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/omaha-world-herald/191635394/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> Bruning ultimately defeated Avery by a wide margin, receiving 55 percent of the vote to Avery's 45 percent.<ref name="1996 results"/>

==Post-legislative career==
In 1998, Avery was elected to the Gretna Board of Education.<ref>{{cite news|last=Dahlheim|first=Gregg|title=Voter registration sets record in Sarpy|newspaper=Gretna Guide and News|date=November 2, 1988|location=|page=1|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/gretna-guide-and-news/191636065/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> He was re-elected in 2002 unopposed,<ref>{{cite news|last=Carnes|first=Michael|title=Local races are decided before vote|newspaper=Gretna Guide and News|date=November 6, 2002|location=|page=1|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/gretna-guide-and-news/191636814/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> and in 2006.<ref>{{cite news|last=Sloan|first=Karen|title=Slim victory for Gretna sales tax proposal|newspaper=[[Omaha World-Herald]]|date=November 8, 2006|location=|page=20|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/omaha-world-herald/191637068/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref>

Following his departure from the legislature, Avery served on the board of the [[Christian Coalition of America|Nebraska Christian Coalition]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Hammel|first=Paul|title=Voter Guide Won't Be Issued|newspaper=[[Omaha World-Herald]]|date=November 4, 2000|location=|page=55|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/omaha-world-herald/191637181/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> In 2000, Avery led a group of voters that placed Measure 415, an initiated constitutional amendment imposing term limits on state senators,<ref>{{cite news|last=O'Hanlon|first=Kevin|title=Once again, petitions seek to limit terms for state senators|newspaper=[[Grand Island Independent]]|date=April 27, 2000|location=|page=6|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-grand-island-independent/191637270/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> on the ballot, which was ultimately ratified.<ref>{{cite news|title=Voters approve same-sex marriage ban|newspaper=[[Star-Herald]]|date=November 8, 2000|location=[[Scottsbluff, Nebraska]]|page=5C|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/star-herald/191637401/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref>

In 2002, following Bruning's election as [[Attorney General of Nebraska]], Avery applied for his vacant seat,<ref name="nine republicans"/> but Governor [[Mike Johanns]] ultimately appointed Ray Mossey.<ref>{{cite news|last=Reed|first=Leslie|title=Bruning's seat goes to Mossey|newspaper=[[Omaha World-Herald]]|date=November 15, 2002|location=|page=13|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/omaha-world-herald/191636753/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref>

Avery ran for a position on the Learning Community Coordinating Council for [[Douglas County, Nebraska|Douglas]] and [[Sarpy County, Nebraska|Sarpy]] counties, which oversaw the school districts within both counties.<ref>{{cite news|last=Young|first=JoAnne|title=Learning Council attracts ex-senators|newspaper=[[Lincoln Journal Star]]|date=July 17, 2008|location=|page=1B, 2B|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/lincoln-journal-star/191637532/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> He was elected in 2008,<ref>{{cite book|title=Official Report of the Board of State Canvassers of the State of Nebraska, General Election, November 4, 2008|last1=Gale|first1=John A.|publisher=Nebraska Secretary of State|date=2008|url=https://sos.nebraska.gov/sites/default/files/doc/elections/2008/2008%20General%20Canvass%20Book.pdf|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Robb|first=Jeffrey|title=Six spots open on learning council|newspaper=[[Omaha World-Herald]]|date=November 18, 2008|location=|page=1B, 2B|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/omaha-world-herald/191637625/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> and re-elected in 2012,<ref>{{cite book|title=Official Report of the Board of State Canvassers of the State of Nebraska, General Election, November 6, 2012|last1=Gale|first1=John A.|publisher=Nebraska Secretary of State|date=2012|url=https://sos.nebraska.gov/sites/default/files/doc/elections/2012/2012-general-canvass.pdf|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> and 2016.<ref>{{cite book|title=Revised Official Report of the Board of State Canvassers of the State of Nebraska, General Election, November 8, 2016|last1=Gale|first1=John A.|publisher=Nebraska Secretary of State|date=2016|url=https://sos.nebraska.gov/sites/default/files/doc/elections/2016/2016-canvass-book.pdf|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref> He did not seek re-election in 2020.

==Death==
Avery died in [[Omaha, Nebraska]], on August 30, 2023.<ref>{{cite news|title=Avery, Michael Thomas (February 15, 1952 - August 30, 2023)|newspaper=[[Omaha World-Herald]]|date=September 13, 2023|location=|page=B3|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/omaha-world-herald/191636471/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=February 18, 2026}}</ref>
